Messages.Author: noodleboy
Messages.Body:
All moaning about how lame it is that Crusades are Rare [and I must
side with the moaners on this one - pulling a Crusade out of a booster
I paid good dollars for makes me want to gouge someone's eyes out]
what ever happened to the old Archbishop vs Princes rule that existed
when the Sabbat set first came out?

Now that all the Euro cities are being brought out as Crusades,
wouldn't it be a good idea to bring back the old "Archbishops and
princes contesting control of a city can rush each other as a D
action" rule?

I always thought that rule added a lot of flavour to the game, on the
rare occasion that a contestation actually occured.

nood

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:


Oh, never mind the advantage to combat decks. It was just a stupid
rule, both in terms of the backstory and the card game.

In terms of the backstory, the thing made no sense whatsoever! I
love it: Dragos gets elected Archbishop of Atlanta and as they're
showing him the ropes in his new domain, his assistant hands him
some keys and says, "Oh, by the way, here's the key to the
passage way."

"Passage way?"

"Oh, yea. As Archbishop of Atlanta, you now have a secret passageway
that runs directly between your office and Rake's office. You guys are
practically roommates now. Wanna go see him right now?"

I mean, what the hell is this? Clue? I didn't know Mrs. White in the
Lounge could get elected Prince of Miami, grab the lead pipe, and go
take a run at Archbishop Mustard in the Conservatory with a rope - just
the two of them, vampire-to-vampire. I mean, it's not like title-holders
have anyone working for them, preventing the opposing leader from
just waltzing into their haven any time he feels like.

In terms of the game, all does is create the potential for another one of
those random, unplanned fucks. "Hey, great!" Having brought out Fleurdumal,
I see where my prey has gotten elected Dragos to pass a Crusade: Miami
using a Dia de los Muertos. Oooh! Bad play on my part!!!" I mean, what
is the strategy against this supposed to me. (And if you say, "Never use
princes.", please proceed directly to another thread where they don't care
about the real world.) I realize this game already has random, unplanned
screw plays a plenty built in. But we don't need any more such devices.
The current rule is nice, moderate, and reasonable and does the trick
just fine.

Fred

Messages.Author: Opa Opa Jr
Messages.Body:
*sigh* i miss the old rule. it made more sense. sure they are competing for
the same city, but they aren't contesting the same title, as in
archbishop=!prince. i thought the short, but sweet answer on the sabbat
boosters was wholly logical. sure they are vying for the same city, but they

Messages.Author: Opa Opa Jr
Messages.Body:
Still agree with Martin here. Sure many titled camarilla are not battle
monsters. But that doesn't mean they are helpless before the onslaught.
They've always, like martin pointed out, had to deal with rushes and they've
always had a panalopy of ways to deal with it (no sense going into it
again). There's plenty of types of rushes available now and risking
titled-to-titled ocmbatants is not such a high priority in deck design. This
other form of rush is so conditional as to hardly be a detriment.

Remember there's only so many turns in a game and therefore only so many
actions. In fact returning the old rule would give strength to vote decks
because they'd have more turns (and therefore actions and chances to vote)
with their competing minion. A non-combat vote deck can handle combat
evasion and blood bloating easily, so I really have trouble seeing the
concern here. In fact, if anything, combat decks should be happy the rule
exists because contestation is a great way to tie up an annoying vote
monster.

I'm for the joy of atmosphere. I think the rule should come back.

Right. Now explain the point where only the Archbishop gets to readily
attack the Prince and vica versa. Stupid, makes no sense whatsoever.

If you had created a game where titled vampires may always be rushed
by opposing vampires, that would make sense per the explanation you're
pushing above. (Or, for instance, you could make a subset of titles
"rushable", under varying conditions.) However, that would make a much
different game than what we've got now. And it's much different than
THIS: "I happen to have vampire A, the Archbishop of X. You happen to
have vampire B, the Prince of X. Vampire A can specifically rush
vampire B and vica versa." No other combinations allowed. And therefore
complete happenstance, as no one would ever bother to design a deck around
this feature. Happenstance, though not entirely avoidable, is a poor
attribute for a strategy game rule.

Fred

Not on that order. You can always yield the title if you don't want

and win the title that way. *Much* better than, "OK you two vampires
are allowed to rush each other." And it makes a lot more sense in the
backstory, if one cares about such things.

Fred

Sure, why not? Perhaps you were assume "Fame" had to mean something
like an internationally famous singer going on concert tours? How
about a reclusive author who's written lots of popular books? OTOH,
a vampire torporized in a fight is left in heap wherever the fight was.
Watch where the thrown cars came from.

> > How so?
>
> You say that vampires who contest titles being able to rush each other is

> a rule that no one can strategize for, and so should be avoided, and
> then go on to say that contesting titles -- which is a rule that no one
> can strategize for -- is fine, because, hey, if one of the decks is a
> combat deck, it can play a rush card to knock the other vampire into
> torpor...

Having the same title is happenstance either way, no matter what the
game rule about it says, obviously. So the grounds of your accusation of
self-contradiction boil down to the point that I prefer the current rule
rather than the original rule. This is ludicrous. The point of the
"happenstance" argument is to note that this condition comes up not
because it can be strategically planned for or made to come up, but
because it simply comes up at random from time to time for various
reasons. Therefore it is not a thing that should be given a strong type
of effect which varies wildly in the advantages and disadvantages it
grants based on the type of deck one chooses to bring. As I've posted
elsewhere on the thread, allowing the two to simply contest the titles
as you would if they were in the same sect is a much milder and more
generic effect than giving each a permanent Contract on one another.
(And by calling it a "Contract on one another", note that the Prince and
Archbishops are the HIRED ASSASSINS in this role, not the ones taking
out the contracts on one another, as might be a lot more intuitive.)

Fred

into account properly. I don't play the role game and the only fiction
I've read are the clan novels and a few of the mid-90s werewolf novels.

One thing about VtES is that there's some abstraction going on, which
leads to these little disputes like I'm having Colin and others. He
abstracts this in his mind one way and I apparently abstract it in another.
When I think of torpor, I think of the kind of thing that happened to
Vegal, left lying in a heap for Leopold to readily diablerize. I guess
some torpor situations are much different, particularly with ancient
vampires. But I don't have enough experience with either the RPG or
the fiction to have much idea how that would work. I've always assumed
the Jyhad abstraction was much more the former than the latter.

Fred
